texto: Truly a really great crime thriller with some striking imagery and cinematography (seeing the night vision goggle POV and watching Jodie Foster scramble around mere millimetres from the killer’s grasp is true genius) but in principle I cannot rate this highly because of how uncomfortable the portrayal of transness made me. The script tries to absolve itself with a throwaway line about how ‘not all trans people’ are sadistic killers, but when the climactic shot is a shattered window casting daylight over the American flag, after white lady has finally vanquished twisted man-who-wears-ladies’-skin, it’s hard not to think of terf rhetoric (taking a moment to say fuck JK Rowling!!!). Like how Texas Chainsaw uses men in women’s clothing to show the collapse of tradition in America post Vietnam War, Silence of the Lambs takes it a step further by directly pointing the finger at trans folk, becoming  another movie where queerness and transness are used as foils for perceived cultural decline/ perversion. Not a groundbreaking observation I know, but I think important to call out because it’s often so well disguised in crime/horror. The genre wants the viewer to feel uncomfortable, but it’s important to critique the root of that discomfort and ask whether it’s actually tapping into subconscious (or conscious!) prejudices. Also sorry but when we’re supposed to be disturbed by the reveal of Buffalo Bill in full geish pussy facing the world she looks … sickening ? I was gagged tbh.

So I finally watched this juggernaut of a horror icon, and my thoughts are... mostly neutral. The thing that I liked the most was just Clarice, I liked watching her and learning about her. Every other character- including Hannibal- didn't really grab me the way Clarice did. In terms of horror protagonists, she's going up there for me. I think Hannibal as a character came off so dull to me because I've seen his archetype in fucking every villain that's written to be some kind of master manipulator in the past 20+ years. Not only that, but I think media really exaggerates the idea of a genius serial killer. Like, serial killers are primarily cis men not because theyre good at outwitting the police, but its because the police dont give a shit and would rather pretend serial killers are this entirely different breed of human thats as smart as a super computer to avoid accountability. We also just live in a society that frequently lets men off the hook and doesnt believe victims. You can also imagine why depicting a trans-coded character as this type of 'inhuman monster' is pretty egregious, but that's another thing. Anyway, this tendency to believe serial killers are highly intelligent also means that some people gravitate towards these characters as some kind of role model due to their coolness, and they are some of the most insufferable people I have met... Probably because fascists love this shit mostly (not saying everyone who likes villains are fascists btw, i dont think youre weird if you like Hannibal). When a character is being portrayed as impossibly intelligent/powerful and acknowledged as such, all while committing such heinous violence is like candy to fascists, I mean you can look at dozens of characters that fascists like to 'claim' and they'll usually fit that profile to a degree. So, when I see Hannibal, I see a completely fictitious idea of a serial killer invented by lazy cops and held up as this badass supervillain by obnoxious men, and perpetuates certain pop psychology bullshit that still has not gone away. On top of that, I was on Tumblr in 2014 when people would not shut up about the TV show and the Hannibal/Graham ship. So honestly Hannibal Lecter was ruined for me by virtue of me being born in 2001 lol. It's also surprising but not really that I have never heard anyone mention the themes of misogyny in this movie. The only thing I see people reference from this movie is Hannibal and the transphobic caricature, which is darkly ironic. I just wish this movie didn't boil down to a cis woman proving herself by killing transfem-coded character as some kind of like, feminist moment to prove all her male coworkers wrong. I saw someone call this a TERF movie and I agree with that sentiment. I'll give them a point for trying to specify that Bill isn't a transwoman "because trans people aren't violent", but one single line is pretty pathetic. So, the transphobia is the primary reason I'm giving it a low rating, it's too tied into the movie's themes for me to ignore or look over. I admit it's a well made and compelling movie, but the transphobia is just too severe.

The Silence of the Lambs: A Detective Story Where We're Ahead of the Detective I didn't like The Silence of the Lambs, not one bit. The only thing that works is Clarice's relationship with Hannibal Lecter. Their scenes are the only ones with real tension, because Lecter is so psychotically dangerous that I was genuinely scared of him, and scared for her. Everything else lost me. The biggest problem is information control. The film shows us the killer and his point of view early on, so we already know who he is and what he's doing. In a detective story, we're supposed to solve the case alongside the detective. Here the narration is unrestricted, and Clarice spends the whole movie playing catch-up with the audience. She has the clues, but she takes so long to put them together that she comes off as smart and dumb at the same time. There's no mystery left to solve, only waiting for her to reach where we already are. Then the film flips it and leaves us out of things we actually need to know. Take the fake deal with Lecter. We never see the plan being built between Clarice and the FBI director, so it plays as a confusing twist instead of suspense. If we had known the deal was fake ahead of time, every scene with Lecter would have carried the question of whether he'd see through it. That's Hitchcock's bomb under the table, and the film skips it. The same goes for her power as a trainee. How much is she actually allowed to do? The exposition we need is missing, and the exposition we don't need, the killer's identity, arrives too early. Structurally, it's a mess. The A plot and the B plot keep trading places. It starts as a Hannibal Lecter film, then turns into the serial killer film, then forgets Lecter until the very end. The two threads overlap instead of building on each other, so I never knew where the story was. The structure is loose, and the case never held me. The climax leans on plot convenience. Clarice ends up alone in the killer's house, and the film only gets her there by sending the FBI to the wrong place. Why is a trainee walking into that without backup? It's a contrivance to strand her, and it made the ending feel dumb instead of tense. That ending also undercuts her character. I get that she's a rookie, a woman in a man's field, and terrified. But the performance in the house is so heightened that it feels performative, with no sign of the training the film keeps telling us she has. Throughout the film she reads as too small and too weak. I didn't need her to be fearless. I needed her to try to take control. Without that, I didn't believe her, and I didn't have much rooting interest in her. Apart from Lecter's escape and the conversations between the two of them, the film never frightened me the way I expected. For a movie this celebrated, I just don't understand the popularity. It lost me.

Got myself the Criterion 4k and it has revealed to me that this is a perfect film. It’s a genuinely upsetting watch. I’m not ashamed to admit I cried for about the runtime. Scott Glenn is pretty good as Jack Crawford but nothing crazy. Anthony Hopkins is obviously fantastic; his cold, piercing blue eyes that calculate your every thought paired with his stiff, imposing presence and quiet, sadistic glee make him a terrifying devil to deal with. Ted Levine is horrifying in a completely different way, he brings a much more twisted humanity and rage- an intentional need to hurt. However, my favorite performance and the real heart of this film is in Jodie Foster. Her performance as Clarisse Starling is one of the best I’ve ever seen. One of those rare performances that I just don’t know how to describe. She puts so much into the character it’s like reading a book. In the titular scene, where she is in some sort of dark therapy session with Dr. Lecter, we are only shown the two actors faces, tight and mirrored in between the bars. And with just her voice and eyes, boosted by the Howard Shore score, Foster paints an image so vivid I had to check to make sure there wasn’t anything intercut. I can see the moon shining through her bedroom window when she wakes to the horrific sounds coming from the red barn outside, lights burning inside it and casting shadows of slaughter. Clarisse is tragically and incredibly heroic. She manages to save one lamb, but even the rescued lamb is never the same. The slaughter continues despite her best efforts. Speaking of that Shore score; to me it is our musical cue for when Clarisse is hearing the lambs. I think it says a lot how it continues playing even after Bill is dead. In regards to this movie being an upsetting experience, director Johnathan Demme connects us to Clarisse so thoroughly with his brilliant camera work that we feel everything she does. All the men surrounding her looking like hungry wolves, how much smaller of a physical threat she is, how she gets taken less seriously. It’s one of the more feminist films I’ve really understood. We are always with her, she is almost always center frame. We see her memories, sometimes even get her POV. It’s part of why we love Hopkins’ Lecter so much- he is, albeit still in a somewhat perverted way, the most respectful man to Clarisse. It’s why the ending sequence is one of the greatest ever. As soon as we we get that green POV, we are terrified for her. We become the monster trying to reach out and touch her. We realize just how much power he feels in that moment, and because he underestimates a woman, we watch him catch a clip in the chest. This movie has so many good outfits and great color grading. I’m sure there’s meaning in her wardrobe I’m not picking up on but Clarisse sure can wear a sweater. Those greens and maroons and deep blues are so good; the really complement Foster’s shining green eyes. Demme is really such an incredible director. There’s so much great blocking in this, like in the elevator or moratorium. And so so much power dynamic stuff in the actors’ positioning, particularly in the Clarisse/Hannibal scenes. Also it ends in the Cincinnati area so that’s cool! Best closing line as well. 10/10

The dialogue feels natural but layered with meaning, the pacing is practically flawless, and the screenplay never underestimates its audience.
